_readme: Working English translation of Theon's Progymnasmata, made for this app directly from
the public-domain Greek of Walz (Rhetores Graeci) that build-theon.py ingests. It is an
original translation: Kennedy's SBL 2003 English is under copyright and was not used.
Keys are 'chapter.paragraph', matching the numbering build-theon.py emits.
build-theon.py merges these into the `text` field of each paragraph, and only marks the
work as no-longer-Greek-only once EVERY paragraph has an English rendering — so a
partly-translated work never ships blank English columns to students.
Hand-polish freely; square brackets mark words supplied for sense, and (†) marks a spot
5.1: A chreia is a concise statement or action, aptly attributed to a definite person or to something corresponding to a person. Closely related to it are the maxim and the reminiscence: for every concise maxim attributed to a person makes a chreia, and the reminiscence too is an action or a saying useful for life. The maxim differs from the chreia in these four respects: that the chreia is always attributed to a person, the maxim not always; that the chreia sometimes states a general truth and sometimes a particular one, whereas the maxim states only the general; further, that the chreia sometimes makes a joke and has nothing useful for life in it, whereas the maxim always concerns what is useful in life; and fourth, that the chreia is an action or a saying, while the maxim is a saying only. The reminiscence is marked off from the chreia in these two respects: the chreia is concise, whereas the reminiscence is sometimes extended; and the chreia is attributed to particular persons, whereas the reminiscence is remembered also for its own sake. It is called chreia par excellence because, more than the others, it is useful for many purposes in life — just as, though there are many poets, we are accustomed to call Homer alone “the Poet” par excellence.
5.2: Of the chreia there are three highest classes: some are verbal, some active, and some mixed. Verbal are those that have their force through words, without an action — for example, Diogenes the philosopher, when someone asked him how he might become famous, answered, “By caring as little as possible about fame.” Of the verbal there are two species, the declarative and the responsive. Of the declarative, some are by voluntary statement — for example, Isocrates the sophist used to say that gifted students are children of gods; others arise out of a circumstance — for example, Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, seeing a rich but uneducated youth, said, “This fellow is filth plated with silver”; for Diogenes did not simply make the statement, but out of what he saw. Again, of the responsive there are four species: that by [yes-or-no] question, that by inquiry, that by question with a reason attached, and the one called responsive by the same name as its class. A question differs from an inquiry in that to a question one need only assent or deny — nod or shake the head, or answer with a yes or a no — whereas an inquiry demands a longer answer. An example by question: Pittacus of Mytilene, asked whether a man doing something wicked escapes the notice of the gods, said, “No — not even in intending it”; for what is added after the denial is superfluous, since the denial would have sufficed even if it were taken away. The inquiry type is like this: Theano the Pythagorean philosopher, asked by someone how soon after being with a man a woman may go down to the Thesmophorion pure, said, “After her own husband, at once; after another’s, never.” Those by question with a reason are such as contain, besides the answer to the question, some cause or advice or the like — for example, Socrates, asked whether the king of the Persians seemed to him happy, said, “I cannot say, since I do not even know how he stands in education.” Responsive [in the narrow sense] are those that come neither by question nor by inquiry, but where there is some remark to which the reply is made — for example, once when Diogenes was lunching in the marketplace and called him over to lunch, Plato said, “Diogenes, how charming your lack of affectation would be, if it were not affected”; for Diogenes was not asking Plato about anything, nor is Plato inquiring of him, but simply invites him to lunch, which belongs to neither kind. Besides these there is another species falling among the verbal chreiai, called double. A double chreia is one containing the statements of two persons, either of which by itself, with one person, makes a chreia — for example, Alexander king of the Macedonians, standing over Diogenes as he slept, said, “A man who is a counsellor should not sleep the whole night through,” and Diogenes replied, “— one to whom the peoples are entrusted and who has so many cares”; for it would have been a chreia even so, without the reply added. Active are those that reveal some thought without speech. Of the active, some are agentive and some passive. Agentive are those that show some action — for example, Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, seeing a greedy boy, struck his tutor with his staff. Passive are those that signify something suffered — for example, Didymus the flute-player, convicted of adultery, was hanged by the part his name denotes. Mixed are those that share in both the verbal and the active but have their force in the active — for example, Pythagoras the philosopher, asked how long the life of men is, went up to his bedroom and looked out for a moment, showing by this its brevity. And again, when someone asked a Laconian where the Lacedaemonians have the boundaries of their land, he pointed to his spear.
5.3: These, then, are the species of chreiai. They are delivered: some as maxims, some with proof, some as a witticism, some by syllogism, some by enthymeme, some by example, some as a wish, some symbolically, some figuratively, some by ambiguity, some by a shift of subject, and some in combination, composed of whichever of the aforesaid modes. As a maxim: Bion the sophist used to say that the love of money is the mother-city of all vice. With proof: Isocrates the orator used to urge his pupils to honour their teachers above their parents, because parents are the cause of living only, but teachers of living well — for Isocrates brought out his statement together with its proof. As a witticism: Olympias, learning that her son Alexander was declaring himself the son of Zeus, said, “Will this fellow never stop slandering me to Hera?” By syllogism: Diogenes the philosopher, seeing a youth excessively adorned, said, “If it is for men, you are unlucky; if for women, you do wrong.” By enthymeme: when a companion, Apollodorus, said to Socrates the philosopher, “The Athenians have condemned you to death unjustly,” he laughed and said, “And would you have preferred justly?” — for we must supply the further thought that it is better to be condemned unjustly than justly, which seems to be left out of the chreia though it is conveyed by implication. By example: Alexander king of the Macedonians, urged by his friends to amass money, said, “But these things did not profit Croesus either.” As a wish: Damon the trainer, who was lame in the feet, when his shoes were stolen said, “May they fit the thief.” Symbolically: Alexander king of the Macedonians, asked by someone where he kept his treasures, said, “In these,” pointing to his friends. Figuratively: Plato the philosopher said that the shoots of virtue grow by sweat and toil. By ambiguity: when a boy was being introduced to Isocrates the orator and the one introducing him asked what the boy needed, he said, “A ΚΑΙΝΟΥ writing-tablet and a ΚΑΙΝΟΥ stylus” — for it is ambiguous whether he means a tablet and a mind (καὶ νοῦ), or a new (καινοῦ) tablet and a new stylus. It is by a shift of subject when the one answering transfers what is said and asked to something else — for example, when some men over their drinks were inquiring which was the better flute-player, Antigenidas or Satyrus, Pyrrhus king of the Epirotes said, “For my part, Polysperchon — as a general.” The combined mode plainly comes about in many ways: a witticism may be interwoven with a maxim, or an example with a symbol, or ambiguity with a shift of subject, or generally in as many other ways as a pairing can be made, with two or even more modes taken up into a single chreia — for example, Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, seeing a youth born of an adulterer throwing stones in the marketplace, said, “Stop, boy, or you may hit your father without knowing it”; for the saying is at once symbolic and witty.
5.4: Students are exercised on chreiai by recitation, by inflection, by comment, and by objection; we also expand and compress the chreia, and besides these we refute and confirm it. Recitation is straightforward: when a chreia has been stated, we try to render it as clearly as we can, either in the very same words or in others. Inflection is various: we vary the persons in the chreia through the three numbers, and this not simply, but as one to one, two to two, and several to several; and again two to one, to two, and to several; and further several to one, to two, and to several. For when the chreia has been set out — that Isocrates the orator used to say the gifted are children of gods — we inflect it thus: one to one, “Isocrates the orator used to say that the gifted student is a child of gods”; two to two [in the dual], “The two Isocrateses, the two orators, used to say that the two gifted students are children of gods”; several to several, “The Isocrateses, the orators, used to say that the gifted students are children of gods.” It is clear from these how we shall inflect the other ways as well, for they are transferred into the five cases too. But since some chreiai are verbal, some active, and some mixed from both, and these again have further species, we shall try to teach the inflection of each of them by an example. The nominative presents no difficulty, for each of the chreiai is normally delivered in it. The genitive we shall inflect thus: if the chreia is verbal, we shall add to it “the saying was remembered,” or “a saying is recorded of him when he said.” The former is fitting to append after the whole chreia has been recited — for example, “Isocrates the orator saying that gifted students are children of gods, the saying was remembered”; the second is used in the middle of it, as the statement begins — for example, “Pittacus of Mytilene being asked whether a man doing something wicked escapes the notice of the gods, a saying is recorded of him when he said: not even in intending it.” “A saying is recorded” suits all the verbal chreiai better, except the one by voluntary statement; for that one takes “the saying was remembered.” If the chreia is active: should it be passive, one must add “what befell him was remembered”; should it be agentive, “what was done was remembered”; and similarly with the mixed. Each of these is to be added at the end of the chreia — for example, “Didymus the flute-player being convicted of adultery and hanged by the part his name denotes, what befell him was remembered”; and “Diogenes the Cynic philosopher seeing a greedy boy and striking his tutor with his staff, what was done was remembered.” To the dative, in every chreia except the passive, we shall add “it seemed good,” or “it appeared,” or “it occurred,” or “it came to him,” or something of the sort — for example, “To Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, on seeing a rich uneducated youth, it seemed good to say: This fellow is filth plated with silver.” In the passive we shall add “it happened” — for example, “To Didymus the flute-player, convicted of adultery, it happened that he was hanged by the part his name denotes.” To the accusative we shall add, generally in every chreia, “they say” or “it is said” — for example, “Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, on seeing a rich uneducated youth, they say (or, it is said) said: This fellow is filth plated with silver.” The vocative is clear: we shall address our words to the person as though he were present, to whom the chreia is attributed — for example, “Diogenes, Cynic philosopher, on seeing a rich uneducated youth you said: This fellow is filth plated with silver.” To comment is to approve what has been said in the chreia, aptly and concisely: either that it is true, or that it is noble, or that it is advantageous, or that other men of proven worth held this same view. For example, Euripides the poet said that the mind of each of us is a god. We shall comment from truth thus: “for the mind is indeed a god to each man, urging us on to what is advantageous and holding us back from what does harm.” From the noble thus: “for it is a noble thing that each man should think the god to be not in gold and silver but in himself.” From the advantageous thus: “so that we may not, supposing that what punishes lies far off, have great readiness to do wrong.” From the testimony of the renowned, when we say that a sage, or a lawgiver, or a poet, or some other famous man is of one mind with what was said: for the chreia before us we shall say, “Such is the mind of men upon the earth as the father of men and gods brings on the day.” We object to chreiai from the contraries — as against Isocrates, when he said that teachers are to be honoured above fathers, since fathers furnished us living but teachers living well: for in objecting we say that there could be no living well, had not fathers first furnished the living. One must know that it is not possible to object to every chreia, since many are expressed well and blamelessly — just as it is not possible to praise them all, since with some the absurdity strikes one at once. We expand the chreia whenever we lengthen the questions and answers in it, and any action or experience contained in it; we compress by doing the opposite. A concise chreia, for example: “Epaminondas, dying childless, said to his friends…” — and we need more besides for it. (†) [Refutation may be drawn] from impossibility, as we might say against Isocrates that it is not possible for men to be born of gods, not even if they are gifted; from implausibility, that it is not likely that Antisthenes, an Athenian, having come from Athens to Lacedaemon, should say that he was passing from the women’s quarters into the men’s; from falsehood, that Bion did not speak truly in saying that the love of money is the mother-city of vice, for folly is more so; from the disadvantageous, that Simonides gives harmful advice in urging us to play in life and to be serious about nothing at all; from uselessness, as when what was said should appear of no benefit at all for life; from shamefulness, whenever we show the chreia to be shameful and open to reproach — for example, a man of Sybaris, seeing the Lacedaemonians living laboriously, said he did not wonder that in their wars they do not shrink from dying, since death is better than such a life; for he made his statement in a thoroughly soft manner, and not after a manly fashion. From these topics, then, one must refute; and one must argue against each part of the chreia, beginning from the first, from as many topics as prove possible — for let it not escape us that it is not possible in every chreia to argue from them all.
5.5: We shall arrange the arguments in the same order in which we set out the topics; and the same topics would serve also for the refutation and the confirmation of maxims. Those who are already more advanced should take their starting points from what we shall set out for the theses as well. The introduction must not be of such a kind as to fit other chreiai, but proper to the one at hand; and this will be done well, in the case of the chreia and the fable and all the rest, when we take the starting points of our introductions from one or two of the highest divisions. After the introduction one must set out the chreia itself, and then the arguments in order. Here one should use amplifications and digressions and characterizations, wherever they are possible.
